text: Business logic vulnerabilities (or logic flaws) are design and implementation defects that allow attackers to manipulate legitimate application workflows to elicit unintended behavior. These flaws emerge when developers fail to anticipate unusual application states or enforce business constraints server-side, enabling attackers to bypass purchase workflows, alter transaction-critical variables, or submit out-of-order requests without triggering traditional web vulnerability signatures.

metadata.title: Business Logic Vulnerabilities Core Concept
root_causes: Flawed developer assumptions about user behavior
Failure to anticipate unusual server states
Absence of server-side state and invariant verification
metadata.detection_profile: Low signature detectability; requires domain understanding and context-aware state analysis.

text: Root causes of business logic flaws: 1) Client-side trust bias: assuming traffic originates solely from conforming browser interfaces, leading to weak or absent server-side validation. 2) Inter-component integration assumptions: in complex architectures, engineers make unvalidated assumptions about how auxiliary modules process and sanitize state. 3) Undocumented implicit assumptions: state transitions and precondition constraints are rarely formalized, leaving state machines susceptible to step-skipping and arbitrary transitions via proxy interception.

metadata.title: Root Causes and Mechanism of Logic Flaws
attack_vectors: Direct endpoint invocation bypassing client checks
prerequisites: Application dependence on implicit state sequencing

text: Excessive trust in client-side controls occurs when server-side logic assumes incoming requests originate solely from a conforming browser interface, neglecting server-side validation and integrity verification. Attackers intercept requests via local proxies (e.g., Burp Proxy) to tamper with transaction-critical parameters like price, role, or user ID before processing.

metadata.title: Excessive Trust in Client-Side Controls
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-602: Client-Side Enforcement of Server-Side Security
metadata.flawed_assumption: User input arriving at the backend has already satisfied client-side validation rules.
metadata.impact: Arbitrary parameter tampering, transaction value manipulation, and authorization bypass.

text: Failing to handle unconventional input in numeric fields allows attackers to bypass business invariants and reverse transactional flows. For example, in a fund transfer verification where `transferAmount <= currentBalance`, passing a negative integer (e.g., -1000) evaluates to true and causes balance deductions to function as additions, transferring funds from the recipient to the sender.

metadata.title: Numeric Sign Error and Unconventional Input Handling
metadata.attack_mechanism: Supplying unexpected negative numbers, extreme values, or mismatched types to exploit incomplete server-side domain constraints.

text: Inconsistent security controls arise from the assumption that a user or dataset remains trustworthy indefinitely once initial validation checks pass. Relaxing security checks in downstream components or later workflow steps creates loopholes where authenticated users can invoke operations without ongoing privilege verification.

metadata.title: Assumption of Persistent User Trustworthiness
metadata.flawed_assumption: A user authenticated at step 1 remains authorized and compliant across subsequent operations without continuous re-validation.

text: An encryption oracle vulnerability occurs when an application encrypts arbitrary user-supplied input and returns the resulting ciphertext to the user. An attacker leverages this oracle to construct valid encrypted payloads using the application's internal key and cipher, feeding the forged ciphertext into sensitive endpoints that trust encrypted data without verifying its origin or integrity.

metadata.title: Authentication Bypass via Encryption Oracle
metadata.exploit_path: Arbitrary text -> Oracle Encryption -> Valid Ciphertext Generation -> Injected into Authorization Cookie/Token
compounding_factors: Co-existence of decryption oracle allowing plaintext recovery
Shared key usage between low-privilege input handling and high-privilege access tokens

text: Email address parser discrepancies emerge when different components of an application (e.g., web entry validation, domain routing, and authentication backends) parse RFC-compliant or obfuscated email formats inconsistently. By applying specific encodings or syntax variations, attackers bypass domain-matching rules to register unauthorized accounts for restricted internal domains.

metadata.title: Access Control Bypass via Email Parser Discrepancies
metadata.impact: Unauthorized access to tenant data, internal admin privileges, and organization domain bypass.

text: Business logic flaws occur when an application's design or implementation allows legitimate functionality to be subverted to violate intended business rules. Unlike technical vulnerabilities (e.g., SQLi, XSS) that produce predictable syntax or execution anomalies, logic flaws stem from flawed assumptions regarding user behavior, unexpected state navigation (such as transitioning directly from step 1 to step 3 in an authentication workflow), and failure to validate domain-specific invariants. Because logic flaws utilize valid application syntax, automated scanners cannot identify them through standard signature matching.

metadata.title: Introduction to Business Logic Flaws and Contextual Testing
metadata.detection_profile: Invisible to conventional signature scanners; requires contextual misuse modeling and finite state testing.
root_causes: Flawed developer assumptions about state traversal
Absence of domain-level invariant validation
Lack of fail-closed controls on unexpected transitions

text: Business Logic Data Validation Vulnerabilities (WSTG-BUSL-01) occur when an application validates user input only for structural syntax and basic boundaries (e.g., regex, field length, non-negative numbers) while failing to enforce contextual, relational, and business-logical validity. Unlike conventional input injection, the injected values are syntactically well-formed but semantically invalid within the business domain (e.g., active Social Security Numbers assigned to deceased individuals, impossible geographic allocations, or invalid cross-system routing flags). These flaws manifest primarily at system boundaries, multi-tier handoffs, and asynchronous integration queues where downstream components blindly trust upstream data without independent contextual verification.

metadata.title: Contextual and Semantic Business Data Validation Flaws
root_causes: Reliance on syntactic Boundary Value Analysis (BVA) without semantic verification
Implicit trust at cross-system handoff points
Desynchronized business states between distributed tiers

text: Testing Ability to Forge Requests (WSTG-BUSL-02): Applications that rely on client-side state flags, hidden form inputs, predictable incrementing IDs, or undocumented debug toggles are vulnerable to business logic bypass via forged HTTP requests. Attackers use intercepting proxies to submit parameter states that deviate from normal client execution flows. This allows bypassing multi-stage transactional constraints, repeatedly applying single-use business rules (such as discount coupons or credit awards), or activating administrative and debugging paths left active in production environments.

metadata.title: Business Logic Request Forgery and Hidden Parameter Exploitation
root_causes: Client-side reliance for state enforcement flags
Predictable or sequential transaction/state identifiers
Undocumented debug or tester flags active in production

text: Testing Integrity Checks (WSTG-BUSL-03): Applications often determine UI presentation dynamically by hiding, disabling, or rendering certain fields as read-only (such as drop-down selectors, read-only price/quantity text, or administrative fields) based on user roles or contextual state. A business logic integrity vulnerability arises when server-side handlers fail to enforce relational edits and backend authorization checks on incoming parameters, assuming that because an element cannot be edited in the browser, it cannot be submitted. Attackers utilize intercepting proxies to inject or mutate restricted, hidden, or out-of-scope relational values (e.g., unauthorized project IDs, administrative password parameters, or conflicting relational status attributes), subverting data integrity and bypassing authorization workflows.

metadata.title: Business Logic Relational Integrity and UI Inconsistency Vulnerabilities
root_causes: Relying on client-side non-editable controls for business integrity
Omission of server-side relational constraint checks
Implicit trust in submitted hidden parameters

text: Testing for Process Timing (WSTG-BUSL-04): Applications exhibit timing-based logic vulnerabilities in two primary dimensions: side-channel information leakage via execution latency differences, and state machine flow subversion via extended transaction lifecycles. Execution timing variations (e.g., differential authentication response times between valid vs. invalid usernames due to conditional password hashing) allow attackers to infer backend processing state without explicit UI disclosure. Concurrently, missing session or transaction expiration windows allow attackers to stall transactional workflows, gaming dynamic pricing models or locking shared resources indefinitely.

metadata.title: Process Timing and Execution Window Vulnerabilities
root_causes: Non-constant-time execution paths in security-sensitive operations
Absence of hard expiration limits on transactional state holds
Failure to revalidate time-sensitive pricing quotes prior to checkout settlement

text: Testing Number of Times a Function Can Be Used Limits (WSTG-BUSL-05): Applications frequently implement rate limits, invocation quotas, or single-use constraints on sensitive actions where repeated execution accords unearned financial, resource, or operational benefits (e.g., applying single-use promotional discounts, redeeming vouchers, or accessing limited subscription downloads). Vulnerabilities arise when backend controllers rely on transient client navigation flow rather than persistent server-side counters and database locks, allowing attackers to replay restricted operations beyond authorized bounds.

metadata.title: Function Use Limits and Quota Enforcement Vulnerabilities
root_causes: Absence of persistent server-side invocation tracking
Client-side assumption of linear page progression
Non-atomic counter checks enabling replay and race conditions

text: Testing for the Circumvention of Work Flows (WSTG-BUSL-06): Workflow vulnerabilities occur when an application fails to enforce the strictly intended, sequential execution of connected operational steps ($S_0 \to S_1 \to ... \to S_n$) or fails to atomically roll back dependent side-effects when an intermediate transaction is abandoned. Flaws emerge when applications either assume users will follow the browser's linear navigation path, or implement validation checks exclusively during initial resource creation while omitting identical verification during secondary lifecycle operations (e.g., updates, edits, and rollbacks).

metadata.title: Circumvention of Workflows and Inconsistent Lifecycle Validation
root_causes: Failure to enforce server-side workflow sequence progression
Non-atomic transactional rollback of auxiliary benefits upon cancellation
Asymmetric validation between resource creation and resource update workflows

text: Testing Defenses Against Application Misuse (WSTG-BUSL-07): Web applications often lack application-layer active defenses and behavioral monitoring, allowing attackers to iteratively fuzz parameters, map authorization boundaries, and execute out-of-order state transitions without detection or throttling. Unlike standard localized defenses (such as isolated SQLi character filtering or account lockout on repeated bad passwords), a resilient application must detect sequences of misuse across disparate endpoints. The absence of holistic detection allows adversaries to conduct unconstrained reconnaissance, exploit business logic flaws, and conduct automated attacks without triggering security response mechanisms.

metadata.title: Absence of Application-Layer Active Defenses and Misuse Detection
root_causes: Lack of behavioral anomaly detection across authenticated sessions
Reliance solely on perimeter WAF or isolated parameter-level input sanitizers
Absence of runtime thresholding for invalid workflow states or repeated business errors

text: Testing Upload of Unexpected File Types (WSTG-BUSL-08): Applications accept file uploads to support functional workflows (e.g., profile avatars, spreadsheets, invoices), but often fail to enforce strict business-aligned file type boundaries. A logic vulnerability exists when the server fails to reject unapproved file extensions, depends solely on client-side controls or easily forged HTTP 'Content-Type' request headers, or omits file content (magic byte) verification. This allows attackers to upload executable scripts (e.g., PHP, JSP), HTML files containing script payloads, or structurally divergent formats that cause data processing errors, server-side code execution, or unintended system mutations.

metadata.title: Upload of Unexpected File Types and Inadequate Type Enforcement
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-434: Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type
root_causes: Relying exclusively on client-side JS or HTTP Content-Type headers for validation
Missing strict file extension allowlists on the backend
Absence of deep content/magic byte verification
Direct storage of uploaded files within public web execution roots

text: Testing Upload of Malicious Files (WSTG-BUSL-09): Applications that accept user uploads often enforce shallow extension filters without validating the true binary contents or scanning for malicious payloads. Unlike WSTG-BUSL-08 (which focuses on rejecting structurally unexpected or unapproved formats), this vulnerability involves uploading syntactically permitted file formats (e.g., JPEG, ZIP, XML, PDF, CSV, DOCX) that embed malicious payloads. Vulnerabilities manifest when the server places executable scripts within the webroot, decompresses unvalidated archives leading to arbitrary path overwrites (Zip Slip), processes recursive entity references (Billion Laughs / XXE), decompresses explosive compression archives (Zip Bombs), or serves active content (PDF/SVG script injection) without antivirus, content transformation, or sandbox isolation.

metadata.title: Upload of Malicious File Contents and Multi-Format Payloads
metadata.vulnerability_class: CWE-434: Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type
root_causes: Absence of malware/antivirus scanning pipelines on ingested files
Permitting user uploads to be stored within executable webroot directories
Unsanitized path handling during archive decompression (Zip Slip)
Unrestricted decompression of high-ratio nested archives (Zip Bombs)
Direct parsing of untrusted external entities in ingested XML/office documents
